about: Facts behind Sommelier Program Level 3 · Advanced Prep (content/manual-l3), from the Court of Master Sommeliers, Americas (CMS-A) website and its resource-library PDFs, read Nov 19, 2026. Our lessons are in our own words; we link to the Court. Each chapter file carries its own facts list as well (with the regional bodies and other sources its writer used).

facts.fact: The Advanced Sommelier Course and Examination is the third step of the Court's four, after the Introductory and Certified, before the Master Sommelier Diploma.
Unlike the Introductory, the Advanced course and exam are held separately; the course must be attended before applying for the exam.

The Advanced Sommelier Course is a three-day program: classroom lectures that give a template for upper-level study and the exam's expectations, plus small breakout tasting sessions with individual feedback.
The Court recommends waiting at least one calendar year after passing the Certified exam before the Advanced course.

Course eligibility: passed the Certified Sommelier Examination; restaurant service or sales experience within seven years (the page says 'at least two (2) of restaurant experience'); currently employed in restaurant, hospitality or the beverage industry; not attended the course before.

Course applicants take the Sommelier Knowledge Assessment (SKA): about 55 minutes, in person at a Pearson testing center, randomized questions across Theory, Tasting and Practical (Hospitality & Service and Business of the Sommelier). Exam applicants do not take the SKA.
The Advanced exam has three sections: Theory (written), Tasting (verbal) and Practical (Hospitality and Service, plus Business of the Sommelier).

Since 2022 Theory is taken first, at a Pearson VUE testing center; passing it earns an invitation to the Practical and Tasting later that year. All three must be passed in the same calendar year, or the candidate starts again with Theory the next year.
Passing requirement: at least 60% on each section within one calendar year.

Exam eligibility (website): at least three years in a restaurant service or sales job within the last seven years; attended the three-day course; currently employed in the restaurant, hospitality or beverage industry.
Forced wait: a first Practical below 40%, a second consecutive Practical below 50%, or a third consecutive Practical below 55% means waiting an extra year. There is no minimum score on the Tasting.
Applications (course or exam, not both) open October 1 and close November 1; a $100 application fee; no letters of recommendation; RALIANCE online training is a prerequisite, included in the fee.

Theory exam: 60 minutes, about 115 questions; multiple choice, short answer, matching, map identification, label identification, ordering lists, vintage and producer knowledge, and applying tasting and service knowledge. No essays, no 'list all' questions, no opinion questions, no costing math (that is in the Business of the Sommelier exam). US and metric units are both accepted. No negative marking. Spelling and accents are not required (hand-graded by Master Sommeliers).
Theory results, scores and feedback arrive within four weeks; feedback gives the overall percentage and performance in key areas.

Theory topics: viticulture, vinification, France (Champagne, Burgundy, Bordeaux, Loire, Alsace, Rhône, Dordogne and Southwest, Provence, Languedoc-Roussillon, Jura and Savoie), Italy's twenty regions, Germany's thirteen regions, Spain (all major regions, Vino de Pago), Portugal, Greece, England, Switzerland, Austria, Eastern Europe and the Caucasus, the Middle East, China and India, the US, Canada, Mexico (Valle de Guadalupe), Argentina, Chile, Uruguay, Australia, New Zealand, Morocco, South Africa, sparkling, fortified (Sherry, Port, Madeira, Marsala, VDN, VDL), sweet, aromatized wines, beer, sake (including polishing minimums) and spirits/cocktails (distillation, base ingredients, aging laws, aperitifs and digestifs).

The Court's study approach: General Theory Topics = breadth, Areas of Study = depth (location, climate, grapes, vineyard, winery, soils...). Two questions for every subject: why does it taste the way it does, and what do I need to know to serve it tableside.

Expected skill set: in-depth theory of major beverage alcohol; world-class formal service (still, sparkling, decanting, beer, after-dinner and by-the-glass; global food and wine pairing; classic cocktails and spirits; benchmark producers and vintages; hospitality and salesmanship); deductive tasting for a broad range of classic reds and whites; complete beverage program management (list content and design, cellar design, purchasing and inventory, staff training including mentoring toward Introductory and Certified, financial management with cost controls and spreadsheets).

Roles the Court lists for an Advanced Sommelier: floor sommelier, head sommelier, beverage director of a single-unit restaurant or hotel; winery hospitality management, retail manager or owner, distributor or importer educator or senior salesperson.

Business of the Sommelier: the first part of the Practical, a timed 50-minute exam. Exercises include tasting and evaluating beverages, costing (wine, cocktails, flights), reading and evaluating inventory sheets, and correcting a beverage list full of mistakes. A calculator is provided. No negative points.

Business of the Sommelier covers program management: assessing pricing, theme and style; marketing and sales; purchasing; costing; audits; list management; inventory management; staff management and training; beverage equipment management.

Hospitality & Service follows Business of the Sommelier: about 15–20 minutes of preparation with the situation, guest notes, menus, wine list and beverage list; two tables per panel with a maître d'; besides cocktails, beverages are poured tableside; candidates may face confrontational guests played by Master Sommeliers.

Tasting exam: six wines in 25 minutes in front of three to four Master Sommeliers; time calls at halfway (12.5 minutes), five minutes and one minute; give one answer (not a range) for sweetness, acidity, alcohol and tannin; describe a compound's aroma, not just its name ('green pepper from pyrazines', not 'pyrazines').

The Advanced and Master deductive format: Sight, Nose, Palate Structure, Palate, Initial Conclusion (grapes, climate, countries, age range 1–3, 3–5, 5–10, 10+ years), Final Conclusion (grape or blend, country, region and appellation, official quality level, official style category where appropriate, one vintage).

Advanced core whites: Albariño, Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc, Gewurztraminer, Grüner Veltliner, Pinot Gris/Grigio, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc and blends, Torrontés, Viognier. Core reds: Cabernet Sauvignon and blends, Cabernet Franc, Carménère, Corvina and blends, Gamay, Grenache and blends, Malbec, Merlot and blends, Nebbiolo, Pinot Noir, Sangiovese, Syrah, Tempranillo, Zinfandel. The list is most of what is poured and may change (dated 03.2025).

Advanced and Master service standards (2025) cover general hospitality, general service, sparkling, decanting, other wine service, beer, sake, aperitif and digestif, cocktail service and food and beverage pairing. Problem resolution: acknowledge, apologize sincerely, act quickly and kindly. Taste pour 1–1.5 oz / 30–45 ml; the ordering guest is served last; sparkling glasses get no more than two pours; decanting is for aeration, sediment or raising temperature by 1–3 degrees.

disagreements: Experience for the exam: the website says three years within the last seven; the theory exam guide PDF says three years within nine (extended from seven due to COVID-19). We state the website's rule and say to check the Court's page.
Experience for the course: the website says 'at least two (2) of restaurant experience' (the unit is missing; read as two years) within seven years.
The forced-wait rule on the website names a third Practical below 55%; the theory guide PDF says a third Theory or Practical below 55%.
